title: Maine Democrats nominate Jackson to challenge Collins for Senate
dek: Maine Democrats gathered in Bangor on Saturday to nominate Troy Jackson, former Maine Senate president, as their U.S. Senate candidate, replacing Graham Platner after he withdrew following a rape allegation. Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from northern Maine, faces Republican incumbent Susan Collins, who has held the seat for 30 years and reported $11 million in cash on hand. Democrats see the Maine race as critical to their effort to net four seats and regain Senate control.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Troy Jackson was nominated as the Democratic candidate for Maine's U.S. Senate race against 30-year incumbent Susan Collins, with roughly 100 days until Election Day and a tenfold cash disadvantage.
bottom_line: Jackson's ability to close an 11-to-1 cash-on-hand gap in 100 days will depend on whether his grassroots momentum can translate to sustained fundraising and whether his evolution on social issues registers with Maine voters as genuine growth or as political repositioning. Watch for whether Collins' spending advantage and incumbency advantage prove insurmountable even in a state trending Democratic at the statewide level.
body: Maine Democrats gathered in Bangor on Saturday to nominate their U.S. Senate candidate for a race Democrats regard as one of their strongest opportunities to flip a seat this fall. With roughly 100 days before voting ends on November 3, the party unified behind Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from northern Maine and former president of the Maine Senate, to challenge Republican incumbent Susan Collins, who has held the seat for 30 years.

The nomination came after Graham Platner, the party's initial candidate, ended his campaign following a woman's accusation that he had sexually assaulted her in 2021. Platner has denied the rape allegation, according to NPR's reporting.

Jackson enters the race with significant grassroots momentum. Nearly every one of his primary rivals has dropped out, and he has already garnered support from the bulk of elected delegates who cast ballots for the nominee. His campaign reported a fundraising haul of more than $1 million since he announced his run, per NPR. That haul stands in sharp contrast to Collins's position: per Federal Election Commission filings cited by NPR, Collins reported $11 million in cash on hand.

Jackson built a following on an economic populist message, rejecting the Democratic establishment and focusing on affordability concerns. According to NPR's reporting, he backs Medicare for All and supports raising taxes on the ultra-wealthy and large corporations. Jackson is also pushing for the abolishment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and an end to U.S. military aid to Israel. On social issues, he is advocating for Congress to pass civil rights legislation protecting LGBTQ Americans and to federalize the right to an abortion.

However, Jackson has changed his views on reproductive rights and LGBTQ issues, moving from more conservative stances during his early years in public office to the progressive positions he now holds. Additionally, reporting by The Washington Post and CNN, cited by NPR, described Jackson as exhibiting a short temper with colleagues during his time in office.

Collins is running in a state carried by Kamala Harris in 2024 and at a moment when many voters have soured on President Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, according to NPR. Yet her advantage in fundraising and name recognition after three decades in office gives her substantial built-in strength. Jackson has just over three months to build his war chest and make his case to voters in what amounts to a rapid campaign launch.

The Bottom Line: Jackson's ability to close an 11-to-1 cash-on-hand gap in 100 days will depend on whether his grassroots momentum can translate to sustained fundraising and whether his evolution on social issues registers with Maine voters as genuine growth or as political repositioning. Watch for whether Collins' spending advantage and incumbency advantage prove insurmountable even in a state trending Democratic at the statewide level.
